title: Hearing George again at Preservation Hall
summary: George had not changed in sound, though the hall was too small for the power of the Bunk band.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Well, then, uh, you—then you didn't hear George again until 62.
I heard George on records, and I wrote some liner notes for a Blue Note album that George did, but I didn't hear him in person until 62.
Then, who was he playing with? Can you remember who he was playing with in Preservation Hall?
Uh, Jim was there. That's all I remember. That's all I remember.

You know, I mean, that, that so-called All-Star band, the guitar and the slow track, they had quite a good band playing there on weekends, I think. They used to have that band on Saturday in the United States.
No. Perhaps it was. I don't know. I know Jim was there.
Did the—how did the music sound then in 62, as compared to your earlier members?

Um, George sounded the same, Jim sounded the same, but I didn't get the feeling of the tremendous size and the tremendous power that that Bunk band had. And I think part of it was due to the size of Preservation Hall. There just isn't enough room to really project. Uh, but the quality, it had exactly the same sound. Yeah. And again, it was this startling thing, like you'd suddenly been thrown in the lake, you know, what's happened? Here it is again. This instant recognition that this is special and fine. And, uh, immediately it knocked out all other jazz for me, except for the Morton recordings.
